newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Curious Hong Kong eyes Chinese soldiers.
newsitem.headline: Curious Hong Kong eyes Chinese soldiers.

text.p: Chinese soldiers preparing on Tuesday for Beijing's takeover of Hong Kong looked from their barracks windows to see television cameras striving for a quick glimpse of what the territory's future guardians are like.
An advance guard of 40 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops arrived in Hong Kong on Monday ahead of the Chinese garrison to be based here after the British colony reverts to China on July 1.
The group, lead by Major-General Zhou Borong, inspected British military facilities the PLA will inherit upon the handover.

The PLA will take over a new naval base on Stonecutters' Island in Hong Kong harbour, the Prince of Wales Barracks in the heart of Hong Kong's Central business district and currently the British military headquarters, and a wide range of other sites.
Television stations desperate for a glimpse of the Chinese soldiers trained their cameras from early morning on the curtained windows at the Prince of Wales Barracks.
A Chinese soldier drawing the curtains for a glimpse of Hong Kong's spectacular skyline found himself staring into camera lenses.
Behind the curiosity in Hong Kong lies the realisation that the soldiers are the first official physical presence of the future sovereign power in the British colony.

"After 156 years the Chinese army is back in Hong Kong," the English-language Hong Kong Standard said. "It is yet another tangible sign of the inexorable march towards Chinese resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong."
Many Hong Kong people fled the mainland following the Communist takeover in 1949, and many remember the PLA's crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
Their arrival on Monday was kept low key, and China has been at pains to calm local fears.
Beijing officials and military leaders have stressed that the garrison is drawn from the cream of the PLA and is drilled on Hong Kong laws and customs.
But the Ming Pao Daily said in its editorial it was not enough for PLA soldiers to simply memorise Hong Kong laws.

"They need to get to know the place, its people and the culture," the paper said. "Common sights in the mainland, such as the preferential treatment soldiers enjoy, will not necessarily be accepted by Hong Kong people."

The PLA soldiers face a major barrier in any effort to get to know Hong Kong better -- their pay. An average PLA foot soldier gets paid just 40 yuan (US$4.80) per month -- hardly enough to buy a beer in a Hong Kong bar.
The garrison's future commander, Major-General Liu Zhenwu, will be paid 1,200 yuan (US$145) a month -- less than the minimum wage of HK$3,860 (US$499) for foreign domestic servants.
